sentences.text: The skull of this dinosaur measures 29 centimeters in length and features a broad, triangular shape.
Distinctive shields located at the rear of the head resemble the form of horns.
Its body armor is made of thin-walled oval cones, with at least two long spines extending from each shoulder blade.
The name Gargoyleosaurus comes from the English word gargoyle, reflecting the creature's grotesque look.
The specific name is a contraction of the first syllables of the discoverers' surnames.
The skull is 29 centimeters long, broad, and triangular with horn-like shields at the back.
Thin-walled oval cones form the body armor, featuring at least two elongated dorsal spines on each shoulder.
Seven conical premaxillary teeth resemble those found in early stegosaurs.
The holotype was found in 1995 at the Bone Cabin Quarry West locality in Albany County, Wyoming.
This specimen was collected by Western Paleontology Labs and is now held in the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Jeff Parker and Tyler Pinegar, employees of Western Paleontology Labs, discovered the ankylosaur skeleton in 1996.
Ken Carpenter and colleagues formally described the type species Gargoyleosaurus parkpinorum in 1998.
Only one fossil occurrence of this genus has been recorded in the scientific database.
The seven conical premaxillary teeth resemble those of early stegosaurs, suggesting a specific feeding style.
Gargoyleosaurus is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
The genus belongs to the family Nodosauridae.
A 2021 phylogenetic analysis by Soto-Acuña and colleagues recovered it as a nodosaurid.
Richard Campbell Thompson's 2011 analysis showed a fairly basal position in Nodosauridae as a relative of Polacanthus.
This dinosaur lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 152 to 145 million years ago.
It inhabited the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, from 152.21 to 145.06 million years ago.
Fossils are found in stratigraphic zone 2 of the Morrison Formation.

It is debated whether Gargoyleosaurus belongs to Ankylosauridae or Nodosauridae, as previous studies supporting Ankylosauridae only used skull data while distinctive Polacanthinae features appear in the postcranial skeleton.
